title: SHE HID A CHILD WHILE A QUEEN MURDERED THE ROYAL FAMILY—AND FOR SIX YEARS, THE ENEMY NEVER KNEW A KING WAS STILL ALIVE
paragraphs: SHE HID A CHILD WHILE A QUEEN MURDERED THE ROYAL FAMILY—AND FOR SIX YEARS, THE ENEMY NEVER KNEW A KING WAS STILL ALIVE

Her name was Jehosheba. She never sat on a throne, never commanded an army, and never received a crown. But one courageous act helped preserve the royal line through which Jesus Christ would eventually come. This is the extraordinary biblical account of the woman who stood between a murderous queen and a child God had not forgotten.
There was a little boy somewhere inside the palace who was supposed to be dead.
His grandmother wanted him dead.
The people who could have protected him were being slaughtered.
And the kingdom of Judah was about to discover what happens when someone becomes so desperate for power that even innocent children are considered enemies.
But in the middle of that bloodshed, one woman made a decision that would change the course of biblical history.
She did not announce it.
She did not gather an army.
She did not wait until the danger passed.
She took a child who was marked for death and hid him.
And for six long years, while a murderous queen occupied the throne, the future king of Judah remained alive because someone had the courage to protect him.
Her name was Jehosheba.
And if you have ever wondered whether the quiet things you do for God really matter, you need to know her story.
Because sometimes the person God uses to preserve something extraordinary is the person almost nobody notices.
And sometimes the most important victory happens long before anyone knows there was a battle.
The kingdom was drowning in blood.
The story begins in 2 Kings 11, following the death of King Ahaziah of Judah.
His mother, Athaliah, saw an opportunity.
Rather than allowing the legitimate royal succession to continue, she seized power through violence.
Scripture records the horror with devastating simplicity:
"When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal." — 2 Kings 11:1, KJV
Read that again.
She destroyed the royal offspring.
These were not foreign invaders threatening her kingdom.
They were members of the royal family.
Her own descendants were among those endangered by her ambition.
Imagine the terror inside that palace.
The footsteps in the corridors.
The sudden realization that royal blood no longer meant protection.
The children who could not understand why they were in danger.
And somewhere in that nightmare was Joash, an infant son of the dead king.
He was part of the family Athaliah intended to eliminate.
He had no army.
No political influence.
No ability to defend himself.
He was simply a child whose existence stood in the way of someone else's desire for control.
And then Jehosheba entered the story.

"But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain." — 2 Kings 11:2, KJV
There is something almost unbearable about the contrast.
Athaliah was destroying lives to secure a throne.
Jehosheba was risking her safety to preserve one.
One woman saw a child as an obstacle.
The other saw a life worth saving.
And the difference between them was not their access to power.
It was what they chose to do with the power they had.
Jehosheba's name deserves to be remembered.
In Hebrew, her name appears as יְהוֹשֶׁבַע (Yehoshevaʿ), commonly understood to carry the meaning "Yahweh has sworn" or "Yahweh is an oath."
Her name is especially meaningful when we remember the promise God had made concerning David's royal house.
In 2 Samuel 7:12–16, the Lord promised David an enduring dynasty. That promise would ultimately find its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the Son of David whose kingdom has no end.
But here, in the days of Athaliah, the Davidic royal line faced a terrifying threat.
A murderous ruler was trying to wipe out the royal descendants.
And the survival of one child became extraordinarily significant.

We must be careful not to claim more than Scripture says. The Bible does not record Jehosheba receiving a special vision or hearing an audible command from God. It does not tell us everything she thought or felt.
What it does tell us is enough.
She acted.
She rescued Joash.
She hid him and his nurse.
And the child survived.
Sometimes we want to know every detail of a biblical hero's heart.
But God has given us something more concrete.
A courageous deed.
A preserved life.
And a reminder that faithfulness can have consequences far beyond what one person can see.
There is another important detail in 2 Chronicles 22:11.
Jehosheba was the wife of Jehoiada the priest.
That passage also identifies her as the daughter of King Jehoram and sister of Ahaziah.
She was not an outsider who happened to hear about the danger.
She belonged to the royal family.
She understood the world in which this violence was unfolding.
And she chose to protect her nephew rather than surrender him to the ambitions of Athaliah.
Think about the cost that choice could have carried.
If her actions were discovered, the consequences could have been deadly.
Scripture does not describe the precise risks she calculated, so we should not invent a secret conversation or a dramatic confrontation that the Bible never records.
But the danger surrounding the rescue is unmistakable.
Athaliah wanted the royal heirs eliminated.
Jehosheba kept one alive.
And then came the six years.
Six years of a hidden king.
2 Kings 11:3 tells us:
"And he was with her hid in the house of the LORD six years. And Athaliah did reign over the land." — KJV
Six years.
While Athaliah ruled Judah, Joash remained concealed in the house of the Lord.
The Hebrew text describes this period using the expression שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים (shesh shanim), meaning "six years."
There is no mystery hidden in the translation.
The weight is in the reality.
Six years is a long time to protect a vulnerable child from a ruler determined to eliminate the royal line.
Six years in which the kingdom appeared to belong to Athaliah.
Six years in which the legitimate heir remained out of public sight.
Six years in which the survival of David's royal house was being preserved in a place associated with the worship of the Lord.
And that detail matters.
The temple was not merely a convenient hiding place in the biblical account.
It was the house of the Lord, the center of Judah's covenant worship.
Yet we should not romanticize the story as though Scripture describes every day of Joash's childhood there.
We are not told how Jehosheba managed every danger, how often she feared discovery, or what conversations took place during those years.
The Bible leaves those details unspoken.
But it gives us the truth that matters most.
The child was hidden.
The child remained alive.
And Athaliah did not succeed in destroying the entire royal line.
Now consider something about your own life.
Have you ever done what was right and then watched someone else appear to win?
Have you ever obeyed God, only to find yourself living through a season that made no sense?
You prayed.
You endured.
You tried to remain faithful.
But the circumstances did not change.
The person who hurt you seemed to prosper.
The injustice remained unanswered.
The promise seemed distant.
And somewhere in your heart, a question began to form.
"Lord, does any of this matter?"
Jehosheba's story does not promise that every hidden season will end with an earthly crown.
It does not guarantee that every painful situation will resolve in six years.
But it does confront the assumption that what is unseen is unimportant.
For six years, the public throne and the surviving royal heir told two very different stories.
Athaliah held political power.
But her power was not ultimate.
And that distinction is something every weary believer needs to remember.
What looks dominant today is not necessarily what will endure.
There are people reading this who have spent years quietly holding their families together.
Mothers praying for children who have wandered from the faith.
Fathers trying to lead their households while carrying private burdens.
Grandparents who keep speaking the name of Jesus over grandchildren who barely understand their prayers.
Husbands and wives choosing forgiveness when resentment would be easier.
Believers fighting temptation that nobody else knows about.
People serving in churches without applause, recognition, or a title.
And perhaps you have begun to wonder whether your faithfulness is too small to matter.
Jehosheba's story asks you to reconsider.
Not because every act of obedience will become famous.
Not because God owes us visible success.
But because the Lord sees what human beings overlook.
Hebrews 6:10 reminds believers that God is not unjust to forget their work and the love they have shown in serving His people.
And Galatians 6:9 encourages us not to grow weary in doing good.
Your obedience does not purchase God's love.
Your sacrifice does not earn salvation.
But the grace that saves us also teaches us to live differently.
Sometimes that difference is displayed in a public declaration.
Sometimes it is displayed in a quiet refusal to abandon someone who needs protection.
Jehosheba was not the king.
She was not the priest who would later organize the royal restoration.
But she performed the act without which the surviving child would not have been there to be crowned.
And that brings us to the moment when six years of concealment finally gave way to public revelation.
The hidden child was brought into the light.
In the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest took decisive action.
According to 2 Kings 11:4–12, he organized the guards, secured the temple, and brought out Joash.
The child who had been hidden was presented to the people.
A crown was placed upon him.
He received the testimony, understood as the covenantal instruction associated with kingship.
He was anointed.
And the people rejoiced.
Scripture records their cry:
"God save the king." — 2 Kings 11:12, KJV
Imagine the shock when Athaliah heard the commotion.
For years, she had ruled.
For years, the royal child had remained concealed.
Now the people were celebrating a king she had failed to eliminate.
She rushed toward the temple and saw what had happened.
The guards.
The gathered people.
The crowned child.
The sound of rejoicing.
And then she cried out:
"Treason, Treason." — 2 Kings 11:14, KJV
The irony is almost impossible to miss.
The woman who had seized the throne through the destruction of the royal offspring accused others of treason when the legitimate heir was crowned.
Athaliah's reign came to an end.
Joash became king at seven years old, as 2 Kings 11:21 records.
The royal line continued.
And Jehosheba's earlier act of rescue now stood at the beginning of a remarkable reversal.
But we must not stop at the coronation.
Because the greatest meaning of this story is not simply that an evil queen lost power.
It is that God's covenant purposes were not extinguished.
And the story of David's royal house reaches far beyond Joash.
There was another King coming.
Centuries after Jehosheba protected Joash, another child would enter a world where a ruler feared losing his power.
His name was Jesus.
Matthew 2 records that King Herod, threatened by news of the newborn King of the Jews, ordered the killing of young boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity.
Joseph, warned in a dream, took Mary and Jesus to Egypt.
The two accounts are not identical.
Jehosheba rescued Joash from Athaliah.
Joseph took Jesus away from Herod's violence.
The historical circumstances and the roles of those involved were different.
But the resemblance is striking.
Earthly rulers tried to secure power through the destruction of vulnerable children.
And those rulers did not succeed in extinguishing God's redemptive purposes.
Yet Jesus was more than another threatened royal child.
He was the promised Messiah.
The Son of David.
The eternal King.
The One to whom the royal promises ultimately pointed.
Matthew 1:1 introduces Him as "the son of David, the son of Abraham."
Luke 1:32–33 declares that the Lord God would give Him the throne of His father David and that His kingdom would have no end.
And here is where the Gospel becomes even more astonishing.
Joash was rescued from death so that he could eventually occupy an earthly throne.
Jesus willingly went to the cross to rescue sinners.
Joash needed someone to protect his life.
Jesus laid down His life for His sheep.
Joash's reign was temporary, and his later life included serious failures, as recorded in 2 Chronicles 24.
But Jesus Christ is the righteous King whose reign will never end.
Joash could not save Judah from the deepest problem of the human heart.
Jesus came to save His people from their sins.
And that is why this story must ultimately lead us beyond admiration for Jehosheba.
It must lead us to worship Christ.
Because the Bible is not merely a collection of inspiring people who made courageous choices.
It is the unfolding revelation of God's redemptive work, culminating in Jesus Christ.
Jehosheba's courage matters.
Joash's preservation matters.
The Davidic covenant matters.
But the greatest King in the story of redemption is not the child hidden for six years.
It is the Savior who conquered sin and death.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because not everyone reading this is living like Jehosheba.
Some of us are struggling with the spirit of Athaliah.
Not because we have committed her crimes.
But because we recognize something uncomfortable in the human heart.
The desire to control.
The refusal to surrender.
The need to protect our position.
The jealousy that rises when someone else succeeds.
The pride that would rather damage a relationship than admit wrongdoing.
Athaliah's violence was extreme and wicked. We must never minimize it by treating ordinary personal struggles as morally equivalent to murder.
But her story still exposes the destructive direction of unchecked pride and ambition.
And if we are willing to be honest before God, we may recognize how easily our own desires can become idols.
We want Jesus to save us.
But sometimes we resist letting Him rule us.
We want forgiveness.
But we struggle to forgive.
We want grace.
But we keep defending the sin that makes grace necessary.
We want a crown without a cross.
And the Gospel confronts us with a question no amount of religious activity can avoid.
Who is truly sitting on the throne of your heart?
Is it Christ?
Or is it the version of yourself that refuses to surrender?
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, a turning of the mind and heart that belongs to a changed response toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because our sins have been exposed.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And even that response is not something we can boast about as though we rescued ourselves.
We come to Christ because we need mercy.
We need forgiveness.
We need the grace of God.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our works.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace or favor.
In the Gospel, it speaks of God's undeserved kindness toward those who could never earn their own salvation.
That means your past does not have to become your final identity.
But it also means grace is not permission to continue comfortably in rebellion.
The same Savior who forgives sinners calls them to follow Him.
To deny themselves.
To take up their cross.
To walk in newness of life.
And perhaps the most important question this article can leave in your heart is not whether you would have been brave enough to rescue Joash.
Perhaps it is whether you are willing to surrender fully to the King who came to rescue you.
Because you can admire Jehosheba's courage and still refuse Christ's authority.
You can celebrate the survival of David's royal line and still reject David's promised Son.
You can read about a hidden king and still keep the true King outside the doors of your life.
Please do not let that be the end of your story.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures.
And He calls people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
You do not need to pretend you are righteous before coming to Him.
You need to acknowledge that you are not.
You do not need to manufacture a spotless history.
You need the Savior who cleanses sinners.
And you do not need to remain chained to the shame of yesterday.
In Christ, forgiveness and a transformed life are possible.
That is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is the heartbeat of redemption.
A palace stained by murderous ambition did not prevent the preservation of a royal heir.
A world stained by human rebellion did not prevent the coming of the promised Savior.
And your life, however complicated its history, is not beyond the reach of the grace of Jesus Christ.
But grace does not mean every consequence disappears.
It does not mean every relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
It does not mean every earthly wound will heal immediately.
It means that through Jesus Christ, sinners can be reconciled to God and begin a genuinely new life.
And that is a greater miracle than receiving an earthly crown.
Maybe you have been hiding behind a smile.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong, but your prayers have become exhausted whispers.
Maybe you have spent years carrying guilt that you never confessed.
Maybe you once loved Scripture, but the noise of life has slowly drowned out your hunger for God.
Or maybe you have been serving faithfully and have quietly begun to wonder whether anyone sees.
The answer is not to make Jehosheba your savior.
The answer is to look to the Savior whose coming her story helps us understand.
Christ sees.
Christ knows.
Christ calls.
And Christ is worthy of your trust.
Bring it before the Lord.
Not to impress strangers.
Not to prove your salvation.
But as an honest expression of your desire to stop pretending and start surrendering.
There are moments when three honest words are more meaningful than a hundred religious sentences.
Someone reading may need to be reminded that the Lord is still merciful, still faithful, and still worthy of trust.
Do not underestimate what a truthful testimony can do in the life of someone who feels alone.
And do not underestimate the importance of helping biblical truth reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
That is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell salvation.
Not to suggest that a Facebook page can substitute for the fellowship, pastoral care, worship, and accountability believers need.

But to use the opportunities God has given us to share Scripture, explain the Gospel, encourage struggling believers, challenge spiritual complacency, and help people grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
Every article takes work.
Every biblical explanation deserves careful study.
Every message of encouragement is an opportunity to point another person toward the truth.
And this work can continue reaching more people when readers choose to stand alongside it.
Biblical giving is not supposed to be driven by guilt.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not one pressured into giving reluctantly.
Not because you must pay to glorify God.
You glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, worship, generosity, and a life surrendered to Him.
But if you believe in this mission, supporting it financially is one meaningful way to participate in helping it continue.
These resources are part of our desire to make spiritual nourishment and biblical learning accessible to people who are hungry for the Word of God.
And there is another way you can help that does not cost anything.
Not simply because we want another share.
But because somewhere in your circle of friends is a person who may be quietly losing hope.
Someone who feels forgotten.
Someone who thinks their years of faithful service have accomplished nothing.
Someone who needs to hear that the throne of this world is not the final authority.
Someone who needs to encounter the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
There is room for honest questions.
There is room for repentance.
There is room for people who are still learning what it means to follow Jesus.
And there is always a reason to keep pointing one another back to Scripture.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that admires a ministry.
The goal is to make much of Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave, remember the woman at the center of this story.
Jehosheba.
A woman whose name many believers have never heard.
A woman whose recorded act of courage occupies only a small portion of Scripture.
A woman who rescued a child when a queen was destroying the royal family.
She could not have seen every chapter that would follow.
She did not know how every future king would rule.
She did not live to read Matthew's Gospel and see the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
But her act became part of the history through which the Davidic royal line continued.
And that is a beautiful reminder.
You do not need to understand every future consequence of obedience before you obey God today.
You do not need a platform to be faithful.
You do not need a crown to serve the King.
You do not need public recognition for your love to be real.
Sometimes obedience looks like protecting the vulnerable.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to cooperate with evil.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth when silence would be safer.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible again after months of spiritual dryness.
Sometimes it looks like confessing a sin you have been defending.
Sometimes it looks like kneeling beside your bed and saying, through tears, "Jesus, I cannot keep living without You."
And if that is where you are today, do not wait for a more dramatic moment.
Turn to Christ now.
Not because your obedience will make you worthy of His love.
But because His grace is sufficient for sinners who come to Him in faith.
The royal child Jehosheba rescued eventually emerged from hiding and received an earthly crown.
But the greater Son of David, Jesus Christ, has already conquered the grave, and His kingdom will never end.
That is the King we proclaim.
That is the grace we need.
That is the Gospel worth sharing.
And that is the hope that can carry us through seasons when faithfulness feels invisible.
The world may never know the name of the person who helped preserve your faith, but the King who wore a crown of thorns will never forget a single act of love done in His name.
